title: Back to the Shower
question: Why did we oscillate, and how close to the edge are we?

blocks.text: I put our drone PID on the shower (same snappy feel, scaled to knob units). It swung hot, cold, hot… just like Mika in Chapter 0. The drone never did that!
The drone has no big delay. The shower has 2.5 seconds of pipe. Let's finally work out what a delay *does*.

The shower has two slow parts: the **pipe**, a pure 2.5 s delay, and the **smoother**, the head and pipe walls warming up with Chapter 3's time constant, $\tau = 1$ s (after 1 s it has closed 63 % of the gap to a new temperature).

First, a confession about Chapter 0's "normal hand". It turned the knob at a **speed** proportional to how wrong the water felt: knob speed $= k\cdot\err{e}$, with $k = 0.8\,\%$ of the knob per second per °C. A speed proportional to the error means the knob *position* is the pile of past error. That's an **I controller**, with $K_i = k$.
For calculations the knob runs from 0 to 1, so 0.8% of its range is 0.008 knob units. The loop formula below uses 0.008; the sliders display 0.8%. Keep the units with the number.
Wait, so in Chapter 0 I was a PID controller? Well, an I controller. An over-eager one.

sections.title: Delay is a lag in the wiggle

blocks.text: I still think a delay just makes everything *slower*. It shouldn't be able to make anything unstable.

Let's isolate the pipe's **pure delay** first. Imagine a sine wave at the pipe's input travelling to the showerhead with no smoothing: the output has the same shape, 2.5 s late. How late is that, *compared with one wiggle*?
Wait. At a 5-second wiggle the hot water arrives exactly when the knob asks for cold. That's not *slower*. That's *backwards*.

The pipe delay stays at 2.5 s, but its **phase lag** depends on how fast the wave wiggles. Call the lag $\phi$ and the delay $L$. If one wiggle takes $T$ seconds (here $T$ is a time, not a temperature), its angular speed is $\omega=2\pi/T$ radians per second. A positive lag means the output trails the input. Engineers write a lag as a negative angle, so the plots below go downwards.
One whole wiggle is one full turn of Chapter 5's spinner: 360°, or 2π radians. So what matters is **what fraction of a wiggle** the delay covers: $L/T$.
A {scrub|L|dis} s delay on a wiggle that repeats every {scrub|T} s covers {calc|frac} of a wiggle, so the output trails by {calc|deg}°, or {calc|rad} radians.
For a 5-second wiggle, 2.5 s is half a wiggle: 180°. In this pure-delay model, each output crest lines up with an input trough. The shower's smoother also shrinks fast wiggles; we'll add that next.
So the same 2.5 s is a nudge for a lazy wiggle and a full flip for a quick one. The pipe never changes. The wiggle does!

This is the spinning arrow from Chapter 5. Delaying the spinner by $L$ gives $e^{i\omega(t-L)} = e^{-i\omega L}\,e^{i\omega t}$: the same arrow, turned back by the angle $\omega L$. With $s = i\omega$ that factor is $e^{-Ls}$, which is why the transfer function of a pure delay is $e^{-Ls}$.

sections.title: Measuring the shower one wiggle at a time

blocks.text: Now add the smoother to the pipe delay. The head and the pipe walls take time to warm up, so the full shower both delays and smooths knob changes. Here's the plan: wiggle the knob at one speed, wait for a steady rhythm, and measure two numbers:

items: **Gain** (the same word as the controller's gain: size out ÷ size in): how big the temperature wiggle is, compared with the wiggle in the water mix we asked for.
**Phase:** how far behind it is, as an angle: its share of a whole wiggle, times 360°.

blocks.text: Each measurement drops a dot on two plots. Measure at least five speeds, slow and fast.

On these plots, each ×10 is one equal step along the axis: 0.1 to 1 takes as much room as 1 to 10. The halfway point between 0.1 and 1 is about 0.3, not 0.55. The ruler is squashed so that a 100-second wiggle and a 3-second one fit on the same plot. Look at the smoother's gain on this ruler: flat for slow wiggles, then sliding down an almost straight line for fast ones, with a bend near $\omega = 1/\tau$.
Equal steps are equal *times*, not equal *pluses*. Like the octaves on a piano!

The smoother shrinks fast wiggles, while the pipe keeps adding phase lag. These gain and phase curves against wiggle speed form a **Bode plot**. Together they are the shower's **frequency response**: how it treats each wiggle speed. Here the input is the **temperature of the mixed water**, so slow wiggles have gain 1. If we used knob fraction as input, the gain would be 45 times larger. To get the frequency response from the formula, set $s = i\omega$: the same trick that found Chapter 9's edge.

blocks.title: What the smoother does to a spinner

blocks.text: Chapter 4's trick again: guess the answer is the same spinner, just a different size and angle.

blocks.tex: \tau\,\dot y + y = u,\quad u = e^{i\omega t},\ y = A\,e^{i\omega t} \;\Rightarrow\; (1 + i\omega\tau)\,A = 1 \;\Rightarrow\; A = \frac{1}{1+i\omega\tau}

blocks.text: Put the spinner $e^{i\omega t}$ into the smoother's rule and the arrow $A$ must satisfy $(1 + i\omega\tau)A = 1$. The arrow $1 + i\omega\tau$ has length $\sqrt{1+\omega^2\tau^2}$ and points up at the angle $\arctan(\omega\tau)$. Dividing by it shrinks by that length and turns back by that angle. Slow wiggles barely notice. Fast ones get squashed and lag towards a quarter-turn, but never past it.
At ω = {scrub|w} rad/s, the smoother (τ = 1 s) keeps {calc|g} of the wiggle and lags it by {calc|lag}°.
At ω = {scrub|w} rad/s the pipe lags {calc|pipe}° and the smoother {calc|lag}°: {calc|total}° in all. {calc|verdict}
Found it! Near 0.95 rad/s the shower on its own turns a wiggle upside down. Remember that speed.

One honest assist: a single measurement can't tell a lag of 90° from 450° (the waves look the same). We count whole extra cycles by following the curve from slow to fast, like tracking one crest through the pipe.

Now close the loop: hand → knob → pipe → skin → hand. Follow a wiggle all the way around. For the Chapter 0 hand, the trip around the loop is $G_{\circ}$ (a little circle for *loop*, because $L$ is already the delay):
My hand piles up error. What does a pile do to a wiggle?

blocks.tex: \int \cos(\omega t)\,dt = \frac{\sin(\omega t)}{\omega} \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \frac{1}{i\omega}:\ \text{a quarter-turn back, } \tfrac{1}{\omega}\text{ as big}

blocks.text: The area under a cosine is a sine, a quarter-wiggle behind: 90° of lag, at *every* speed. And the pile is bigger for slow wiggles, because each hump lasts longer before it cancels: the size goes like $1/\omega$. Chapter 5 said velocity is $i\omega$ times position. Piling up is the reverse: divide by $i\omega$. That's the $k/s$ in the loop.

Feedback subtracts (error = target − temperature). That's a ×(−1), Chapter 5's half-turn, so the wave flips once. If the trip around the loop *also* delays it by exactly 180°, the two flips cancel, and every correction arrives **perfectly in step** with the swing, like pushing a playground swing at just the right moment. If the loop returns the wave at full size (gain 1), the swing keeps itself going; bigger than 1, it grows.

For this simple shower loop, the phase falls through −180° at one relevant wiggle speed. Find that speed on the phase plot, then read the loop gain at the same speed on the gain plot. Is it below or above 1?
At ω = {scrub|w} rad/s the hand's pile lags 90°, the smoother {calc|lag}°, the pipe {calc|pipe}°: {calc|total}° in all. There the normal hand's loop returns a swing {calc|g} times as big.

Slide until the total passes 180°, between 0.45 and 0.46 rad/s. At the exact crossing, about 0.457 rad/s, the swing comes back 0.72 times as big, so the hand could be about 1 ÷ 0.72 ≈ 1.4 times stronger before reaching the edge.

items.def: How many times you could multiply the controller's gain before the loop gain reaches 1 at the −180° speed. Below 1 = over the cliff.
At the speed where the loop gain is exactly 1, how much *extra* lag it would take to reach −180°. More is safer; 45°–60° is a common target (the side trip below says why).

blocks.title: Phase margin is damping in disguise

blocks.text: Why 45° to 60°? Who picked that?

For the simple loops of Chapter 6, phase margin and damping ratio move together. About 43° goes with ζ = 0.4 (25 % overshoot), 52° with ζ = 0.5 (16 %), and 59° with ζ = 0.6 (under 10 %). A margin of 45°–60° is the ζ ≈ 0.4–0.6 sweet spot from Chapter 6, measured in degrees. With a pipe in the loop it is a good guide, not an exact law.

For our shower, the phase of $G_{\circ}$ hits −180° at $\omega \approx 0.457$ rad/s, a wiggle period of about **13.8 s**. The normal hand ($k = 0.008$) has a gain margin of only about **1.4**, and a phase margin of about 22° (where its loop gain is 1, at 0.34 rad/s, the phase is −158°). Close to the edge! The harder hand doubles the gain: 1.4 ÷ 2 = 0.7, **over the cliff**. That's exactly why it never settled.

blocks.q: Suppose the pipe were twice as long (a 5 s delay). What happens to the largest hand gain that's still stable?

options.text: It goes **up**: you can react harder, because you have more time
options.why: More time to react sounds nice, but you're reacting to *older* news. The lag grows at every speed.

options.text: It goes **down**: you must react more gently
options.why: The phase hits −180° at a slower wiggle, and at slow speeds the hand's pile ($k/s$) is big. The loop gain there is larger, so $k$ must shrink: from about 1.12 to 0.60 %/(°C·s).

options.text: It stays the same: delay changes timing, not gain
options.why: A delay doesn't change the size of a wave, true, but it changes *which* speed reaches −180°, and the gain is different there.

blocks.text: With a {scrub|L|dis} s pipe, the speed hand's edge is k = {calc|k} %/(°C·s), and at the edge it swings every {calc|T} s.
Twice the pipe, about half the hand. And the swings at the edge get slower too: almost 24 seconds!
Okay, I take it back. A delay doesn't just make things slower: it eats phase margin, and phase margin is the only thing between you and an oscillation.
Here's your own run from Chapter 0. If your swings were near the edge, their period should be close to what the loop predicts. There's a twist: people are not all the same kind of controller.

A **speed hand** (turn the knob while it feels wrong) is an I controller: its edge is at 13.8 s swings. A **position hand** ("it's too hot, put the knob *here*") acts like a P controller: $G_{\circ}(s) = 45K\,e^{-2.5s}/(s+1)$. A position hand has no pile, so no 90° of its own: the pipe and smoother alone must reach 180°, which happens at a faster wiggle, $\omega \approx 0.95$ rad/s (June's upside-down speed). That means **6.6 s** swings, for any $K$ above about 0.031 knob per °C. Most people are a mix. (The normal robot hand swings a bit slower than 13.8 s, about 15.5 s, because it sits just inside the edge; the harder hand's swings, about 11.6 s, are squashed by the knob hitting its ends.)
A position hand with K = {scrub|K|eff} knob per °C: at the −180° speed (0.95 rad/s) its loop returns a swing {calc|g} times as big. {calc|verdict}
So when I jerked the knob straight to a spot, I was a position hand. My six-second swings were the pipe and the smoother, not clumsy fingers.

Now let’s beat our own hands. The robot uses PI: **P reacts to the current temperature error**, and **I remembers accumulated error**. Together they let the knob respond promptly while I finds the right lasting setting.

The goal: a **phase margin above 45°**, and **10 seconds in the comfort band starting within 12 s**. The slider numbers are percentages of the full knob range: $K_p$ in % per °C of current error, $K_i$ in % per °C-second of accumulated error. The loop equations use knob fractions, so divide the displayed numbers by 100.
Easy. I'll use big gains, like on the drone: fast and snappy. They're already dialled in. Watch this!
…it hunts, hot–cold–hot, every 6 seconds, like a position hand in Chapter 0. Big gains pushed the gain-of-1 speed past the −180° speed. No phase margin at all.

blocks.title: 10 s on paper, 6 s in the shower

blocks.text: June's gains have $K_i/K_p = 1$ per second, which is exactly $1/\tau$. The PI's zero sits on the smoother's pole and cancels it, leaving $2.25\,e^{-2.5s}/s$. On paper that loop reaches −180° at $\omega = \pi/5$, a 10 s swing. But her loop is far past the edge, so the knob slams from end to end, and those slammed swings come about every 6.3 s: close to the position hand's 6.6 s.
The drone could take big gains because it had almost no lag. Here, **robust** means gentle: leave margin for the delay. Try my gentle gains, about $K_p \approx 1$ and $K_i \approx 0.6$.
P reacts to *now*, I to the pile. Adding a little *now* moves the knob a little earlier, which gives back phase: **phase lead**, about 37° at the old −180° speed with Theo's gains.

A well-margined PI gets comfortable in about 9.4 seconds, without repeated large swings. That beats the normal hand (which spent most of a minute swinging before it calmed down) and most humans. It can't beat physics, though: nothing can react to water that hasn't arrived yet. Engineers do have a trick for long delays, a **Smith predictor**, which runs a little simulation of the pipe inside the controller. That's a story for another notebook.

Robustness is the real lesson. Your model of the shower is never perfect: the pipe might be longer, the heater weaker. A margin says how wrong the model may be, as a number you can feel. The phase margin (in radians) divided by the gain-of-1 speed is a **delay margin**: how many seconds of extra pipe the loop can take.
With $K_p$ = {scrub|kp|eff} %/°C and $K_i$ = {scrub|ki|eff} %/(°C·s), {calc|verdict}
The normal hand survives only about 1.1 s of extra pipe. My gentle robot survives 3.5 s. That's what robust means.
Can we just buy a faster heater?

Halving the smoothing time (τ = 0.5 s) lifts the speed hand's edge only from 1.12 to 1.21 %/(°C·s). Halving the pipe (1.25 s) lifts it to 2.06. For a position hand, the faster heater is even *worse*: its edge drops from 0.031 to 0.025 knob per °C, because the smoother was quietly shrinking fast wiggles. Delay is the enemy, not sluggishness.

blocks.title: How the robot actually turns the knob

blocks.text: The robot code writes PI as a knob **speed**: I keeps moving the knob while error remains, and P responds to a *change* in error. At startup, P also gives the knob an immediate move based on the current error. This matches the position rule, except when the knob reaches an end stop.

items: A delay $L$ lags a wiggle by $\omega L$: nothing for slow wiggles, a lot for fast ones.
A pile (I) lags every wiggle by 90°; a smoother by up to 90°; a pipe by $\omega L$, without limit.
Feeding in sine waves and measuring gain and phase gives the **frequency response**; plotted, it's a **Bode plot**, and it's just $G(i\omega)$.
For this simple shower loop, self-sustained oscillation begins when the loop reaches −180° phase with gain 1; larger gain makes the swings grow until limits intervene.
**Gain and phase margin** measure the distance to that cliff. Longer delay means less margin, so you need gentler control.
Our Chapter 0 swings were a controller (us) with too little margin.

items.q: A 2 s delay, and a wiggle with an 8 s period. How much phase lag does the delay add?

options.why: 2 s is a quarter of 8 s, and a quarter of 360° is 90°.
That would be a delay of 1 s. 2 s is a quarter of the period, not an eighth.
That would need a delay of half the period, 4 s.

items.q: On a loop's Bode plot, the phase reaches −180° at 0.5 rad/s, where the loop gain is 0.25. At the speed where the loop gain is 1, the phase is −130°. What are the gain and phase margins?

options.why: The gain could grow 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4 times before it reaches 1 at −180°, and −130° is 50° short of −180°.
Those are the raw readings. Margins are the *distances* to the cliff: 1 ÷ 0.25 and 180° − 130°.
The gain margin is right, but phase margin is the extra lag you could add before reaching −180°: 180° − 130° = 50°.

items.q: Why does a longer pipe force a gentler controller?

options.text: The extra lag reaches −180° at a slower wiggle, where the loop gain is bigger, so the gain must come down
options.why: Right. For an integrating hand, slow wiggles get the biggest boost, so the cliff moves closer.

options.text: The water gets colder in a longer pipe
options.why: We assumed no heat loss. The effect is purely about timing.

options.text: It doesn't: you can react harder since you have more time
options.why: You don't have more time. You have older information. That's the trap from Chapter 0.

items.q: The normal hand has a gain margin of about 1.4. What happens if you react 1.5 times harder?

options.text: The swings grow instead of dying out
options.why: 1.5 is more than the 1.4 margin, so the loop gain at −180° goes past 1: over the cliff.
More gain would only help if there were plenty of margin. With 1.4, there isn't.
Gain is exactly what the gain margin measures, so it definitely matters.

blocks.text: We have every tool now: feedback, PID, poles, margins. Time for the real test: wind, a package drop, and a noisy sensor. **Can you keep the drone at 2 m?**
